## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Dasuttara Sutta* ("Up to Ten") is the thirty-fourth and final discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983; Winternitz 1933]. Ascribed to the venerable Sāriputta, it systematically organizes Buddhist doctrine by enumerating sets of dhammas from one to ten, with ten items assigned to each number, thus totaling one hundred dharmas [Norman 1983; Winternitz 1933; Dhammadinna, ed. 2014]. The discourse represents a structured selection from the preceding *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33) and anticipates the numerical and classificatory methods characteristic of the Abhidhamma [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983; Analayo 2014]. In its section on tens, it notably praises delight in the *abhidhamma* and *abhivinaya* [Analayo 2014]. Because of its analytical mātṛkā-like arrangement and shared attribution to Sāriputta, modern scholars trace close historical connections between the *Dasuttara Sutta* and early Abhidharma-oriented works, particularly the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*, whose opening sections appear to draw directly upon it [Norman 1983; Analayo 2014; Potter 1996].
Four major recensions of the text survive across traditions: the Pali Theravāda version (DN 34); the *Shishang jing* (十上經, DĀ 10) in the Chinese Dharmaguptaka *Dīrghāgama*; an early individual Chinese translation by An Shigao (長阿含十報法經, T 13); and Sanskrit manuscript fragments of the *Daśottarasūtra* recovered from Central Asia (Turfan), which belonged to the Sarvāstivāda *Dīrghāgama* [Norman 1983; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Dhammadinna, ed. 2014; Kuan 2008]. Minor doctrinal discrepancies between these witnesses reflect the sectarian viewpoints of their respective schools, such as the inclusion of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in An Shigao's recension [Dhammadinna, ed. 2014]. SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus both confirm that the discourse shares extensive textual passages across the canon, displaying massive reuse with the *Saṅgīti Sutta*, several books of the *Aṅguttaranikāya* (notably AN 8, AN 10, and AN 5), and the *Vibhaṅga* (Vb 17), alongside close cross-linguistic alignments with Chinese Dīrghāgama parallels (T 1, T 13) and Sanskrit fragments [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
